newsitem.title: CHINA: China calls for end to hostility with Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: China calls for end to hostility with Taiwan.

text.p: China has renewed a call on rival Taiwan to end five decades of hostility between the two sides, the People's Daily said on Wednesday.

"We hope the Taiwan side can...create the necessary atmosphere and conditions...to formally end the state of hostility between the two sides," the newspaper quoted the magazine "Cross Straits Relations" as saying.

It did not say what the necessary atmosphere and conditions were. Chinese officials have in the past said Taiwan's ruling Nationalists, who lost the Chinese civil war to the communists in 1949, must recognise Beijing as the sole, legitimate representative of all China.

Taipei has been keen to resume non-governmental talks, which Beijing suspended after Taiwan's President Lee Teng-hui made a landmark, private visit to the United States in June 1995 in a bid to break the island out of diplomatic isolation.
Beijing regards Taiwan as a rebel province and has sought to push the island into diplomatic isolation.
Bilateral talks had been unofficial in nature to skirt a Taipei ban on official contact with Beijing.

Delicate ties were further strained when China conducted intimidating war games and missile tests near Taiwan in March 1996 in the run-up to the island's first direct presidential elections, which Lee won by a landslide.
"Cross Straits Relations", launched last July to air Beijing's views on Taiwan, said differences between the two sides should not hinder lucrative trade and economic ties.

"No matter what the future of cross-straits talks, the Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Straits (ARATS) will as before promote cross-straits economic and trade cooperation and exchange of visits," it quoted the magazine as saying in its August issue.
ARATS is China's semi-official body for dealing with Taiwan. Both sides espouse eventual reunification, but Taipei says the mainland must embrace multi-party democracy first.
Despite a Taipei ban on direct investment in and trade with China, about 30,000 Taiwanese firms have legally poured $30 billion into China by routing investments through a third country.
Chilly political ties since 1995 have forced Taipei to call for more caution in investing in China, saying the island should not become too dependent on its adversary's economy.

In May, Taipei announced new restrictions on investments in China, but promised to scrap the rules if China renounced the use of force against the island, a threat Beijing has said it would carry out if Taiwan declares independence.
Liu Gangqi, deputy secretary-general of ARATS, is visiting Taiwan, which local media described as a sign of slowly warming relations between the long-time rivals.
Liu, the highest-level mainland representative to visit Taiwan since ties were frozen, blamed the island for more than two years of non-dialogue and sour relations across the Taiwan Strait.
